title: Quiz: Probability Distributions and Transition Probabilities

questions.text: In a Transition Probability Matrix P, what does the entry P_{ij} represent?
options: The probability that the process starts in state i
The probability of moving from state j to state i in one step
The probability of moving from state i to state j in one step
The number of steps needed to reach state j from state i
questions.explanation: P_{ij} is the one-step transition probability from state i (current) to state j (next). The row index i is the 'from' state; the column index j is the 'to' state.

questions.text: For a valid Transition Probability Matrix, the COLUMN sums must all equal 1.
questions.explanation: It is the ROW sums that must equal 1 (not column sums). Each row i gives the probability distribution over next states given current state i, so those probabilities must sum to 1 by the law of total probability. A matrix with columns summing to 1 is called doubly stochastic only if rows also sum to 1.

questions.text: A patient is in the Infected state (I). The one-step TPM gives P_{I,R} = 0.50. What does this mean?
options: 50% of all patients will be in state R next week
A patient currently in state I has a 50% chance of moving to state R in one step
50% of the population starts in state R
The process spends 50% of its time in state R on average
questions.explanation: P_{I,R} = 0.50 is a conditional probability: given that the patient is currently in state I (Infected), the probability of being in state R (Recovered) after one step is 0.50. It says nothing about the global proportion in R or the starting distribution.

questions.text: A stochastic process is called time-homogeneous if:
options: The state space does not change over time
The transition probability P_{ij} does not depend on the current time step n — only on the states i and j
The process always returns to its starting state
questions.explanation: Time-homogeneity (stationarity) means P(X(n+1)=j | X(n)=i) = P_{ij} is the same for all n. The 'rules of the game' are constant over time. This allows us to write the TPM as a single fixed matrix rather than a different matrix at each step.

questions.text: Given the initial distribution π₀ = (0.7, 0.3) and the one-step TPM P = [[0.8, 0.2], [0.4, 0.6]], what is P(X₂ = state 2)?
The n-step Transition Probability Matrix P^(n) can be computed by raising the one-step matrix P to the n-th matrix power: P^(n) = P^n.
questions.explanation: This is a consequence of the Chapman-Kolmogorov equations (proven in Module 2, Lesson 2). By induction, the probability of moving from state i to state j in exactly n steps equals the (i,j) entry of the n-th matrix power of P.
